Uncertainty-aware cloud resource management via fuzzy-adaptive 
hierarchical reinforcement learning
Liwen Chen ID, Chunmao Jiang ∗ , Yanxiao Huang, Wei Wu
School of Computer Science and Mathematics, Fujian University of Technology, Fuzhou, 350118, Fujian, China
H I G H L I G H T S
• Novel FA-HRL integrates fuzzy logic with hierarchical RL.
• Enhances cloud resource utilization by 15 % under uncertainty.
• Reduces task completion time by 25 % compared to state-of-the-art.
• Improves QoS by 30 % with robust workload adaptability.
A R T I C L E
I N F O
Keywords:
Soft computing 
Fuzzy adaptive systems 
Hierarchical reinforcement learning 
Cloud resource optimization 
Uncertainty modeling 
Intelligent decision-making
A B S T R A C T
Cloud resource management faces significant challenges owing to workload and dynamic demands. To address 
these issues, we propose a fuzzy adaptive hierarchical reinforcement learning (FA-HRL) framework that opti-
mizes resource utilization, task completion time, and Quality of Service (QoS). FA-HRL integrates fuzzy logic 
with hierarchical reinforcement learning through three components: a fuzzy workload clustering and prediction 
module, a context-aware fuzzy adaptive reward mechanism, and a fuzzy rule-based policy generation system for 
multilevel decision coordination. Experiments on Google’s cluster traces show that FA-HRL achieves approxi-
mately 13 % higher resource utilization, approximately 10 % lower task completion time, and 30 % improved 
QoS metrics compared to state-of-the-art methods, while maintaining robust performance during workload spikes. 
These results demonstrate the effectiveness of FA-HRL as a scalable solution for uncertainty-aware cloud resource 
management, with significant potential in large-scale cloud environments.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Cloud computing has revolutionized the delivery of scalable, on- demand computational resources, thereby enabling enterprises to achieve unprecedented flexibility and efficiency. However, the Cloud Resource Management Problem (CRMP) remains a critical challenge owing to the inherent uncertainties and dynamic nature of cloud work- loads [ 1 ]. These uncertainties manifest as unpredictable workload fluc- tuations, high variability in resource demands (e.g., peak-to-average ratios exceeding 10:1 [ 2 ]), and complex hierarchical dependencies across virtual machines (VMs), clusters, and data centers. Such dynamics often lead to resource inefficiencies, increased operational costs, or vi- olations of service requirements defined by Service Level Agreements (SLAs). For instance, real-world analyses of Google’s Borg traces re- vealed that 73 % of jobs exhibit a coefficient of variation in CPU demand above 0.85, with peak-to-average ratios reaching 12.6 [ 3 ]. Similarly, Alibaba’s cluster logs indicated that deterministic autoscalers can incur up to 25 % resource overprovisioning or 11 % SLA violations under volatile conditions [ 4 ]. These challenges underscore the urgent need for adaptive uncertainty-aware resource management strategies that can op- timize resource utilization, reduce energy consumption, and ensure QoS compliance in dynamic cloud environments. Traditional CRMP approaches, such as static provisioning and threshold-based autoscaling, are ill-equipped to address these complex- ities [ 5 ]. Static provisioning often results in overprovisioning, leading to wasteful resource allocation and elevated costs, whereas threshold- based methods struggle with delayed responses to sudden workload spikes, causing performance degradation or SLA violations. Huang et al. environments [ 6 ], conventional RL methods face limitations in mod- eling workload uncertainties and coordinating hierarchical decisions across multiple management levels. Similarly, fuzzy logic-based meth- ods excel at handling uncertainty but often lack integration with scalable multilevel frameworks [ 7 ]. The absence of a unified approach that simultaneously addresses uncertainty modeling, hierarchical decision- making, and adaptive learning motivated the development of our fuzzy adaptive hierarchical reinforcement learning (FA-HRL) framework. The FA-HRL framework was designed to tackle three core problems in CRMP: (1) modeling and managing uncertainties in workload patterns and resource demands, (2) coordinating decisions across hierarchical levels (e.g., VMs, clusters, and data centers), and (3) adapting dynami- cally to extreme workload fluctuations. By integrating fuzzy logic with hierarchical RL, FA-HRL introduces a novel solution that combines ro- bust uncertainty representation, multilevel decision coordination, and adaptive policy learning. Specifically, FA-HRL incorporates (1) a fuzzy workload clustering and prediction module to capture multigranularity uncertainties, (2) a fuzzy adaptive reward mechanism to dynamically adjust optimization objectives, and (3) a fuzzy rule-based policy gen- eration system to ensure coordinated decisions. Extensive experiments on Google’s cluster traces demonstrate that FA-HRL achieves up to 13 % higher resource utilization, 10 % lower task completion time, and 30 % improved QoS metrics compared with state-of-the-art methods

sections.heading: Literature
sections.text: review This section reviews prior works on CRMP, organized into traditional methods, RL-based techniques, fuzzy logic and adaptive mechanisms, and hierarchical and prediction-enhanced frameworks. Each section pro- vides a detailed analysis of existing approaches and their strengths and limitations, culminating in a discussion of how our Fuzzy-Adaptive Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (FA-HRL) framework addresses these gaps. Table 1 summarizes the key differences between these methods and FA-HRL. 2.1. Traditional cloud resource management methods Traditional CRMP approaches, such as static provisioning and threshold-based autoscaling, rely on deterministic rules to allocate re- sources. Static provisioning, as described by Buyya et al. [ 8 ], allocates resources based on estimated peak demands, ensuring reliability for predictable workloads but leading to overprovisioning and increased costs in dynamic settings. Threshold-based autoscaling, proposed by Lorido-Botran et al. [ 9 ], adjusts resources by using predefined utiliza- tion thresholds (e.g., scaling up at 70 % CPU usage). These methods are straightforward to implement and suitable for stable workloads but struggle with sudden spikes, resulting in resource wastage or service- level agreement (SLA) violations [ 10 ]. The deterministic nature of traditional methods limits their adapt- ability to the dynamic and uncertain nature of cloud workload. For instance, static provisioning cannot respond to real-time demand fluctu- ations, whereas threshold-based methods often react belatedly, causing performance degradation. These limitations have driven research to- ward intelligent learning-based approaches that can dynamically adapt to varying conditions, as discussed in the following section. 2.2. Reinforcement learning in CRMP RL has gained traction for CRMP owing to its ability to learn optimal policies through interactions with dynamic environments [ 11–13 ]. Deep RL (DRL) approaches, such as Qu et al.’s VM autoscaling method [ 10 ], leverage neural networks to approximate value functions, improve re- source utilization, and reduce latency in cloud systems. Multi-agent RL (MARL) frameworks, such as those proposed by Gari et al. [ 14 ] and Belgacem et al. [ 15 ], enable distributed decision-making and en- hance fault tolerance and load balancing in large-scale data centers. Recent advancements, such as Guo et al.’s integration of imitation learn- ing [ 16 ] and Chen et al.’s actor-critic methods [ 17 ], accelerate policy convergence and improve scalability. Recent advancements in MARL have extended its applications to energy-efficient distributed scheduling. Zhang et al. [ 18 ] proposed a multi-agent cooperative multi-network group framework for the fuzzy flexible job shop scheduling problem, demonstrating improved energy efficiency and scalability in distributed environments. Despite these ad- vances, RL-based methods face challenges in handling high-dimensional state spaces and modeling uncertainties. For example, Qu et al.’s DRL approach struggles with sudden workload spikes because of its reliance on crisp state representations [ 10 ]. Similarly, MARL frameworks lack centralized coordination, leading to suboptimal global decision-making [ 19 ]. Hierarchical RL (HRL), as developed by Mao et al. [ 6 ], addresses scalability by decomposing decisions but often overlooks the uncertainty modeling. 2.3. Fuzzy logic and adaptive mechanisms Fuzzy logic provides a robust framework for modeling uncertainties in CRMP by representing imprecise system states and demands, enabling multi-criteria decision-making akin to Fuzzy Multi-Criteria Decision Making (FMCDM). Haratian et al. [ 20 ] proposed an adaptive fuzzy re- source management approach that dynamically adjusts allocation rules based on workload changes, outperforming traditional k-means clus- tering in reducing SLA violations and directly informing our Fuzzy Inference System (FIS) for balancing resource utilization and QoS. sections.text: This section details the technical design and implementation of the Fuzzy-Adaptive Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (FA-HRL) framework, which addresses the Cloud Resource Management Problem (CRMP). 4.1. Overview of FA-HRL framework The FA-HRL framework comprises three interacting components, as illustrated in Fig. 1 . The first component, the Workload Processing Pipeline, handles incoming tasks using fuzzy clustering and prediction. The second component, the Hierarchical Learning Core, manages the RL across multiple decision levels. Finally, the Policy Optimization Module updates the decision policies using fuzzy Q-learning. The system operates through a coordinated workflow in which in- formation and control signals flow between the components. First, incoming tasks are clustered and predicted using a workload processing pipeline, which forms the foundation for effective resource management. The control loop ensures that the system continuously interacts with the environment, makes decisions, and receives feedback. The optimization process seeks to maximize the expected cumulative fuzzy reward, with con- vergence guaranteed under bounded uncertainty, as demonstrated in Section 5.2.4 ( Fig. 7 ). The computational complexity of the algorithm is analyzed as fol- lows. The per-step complexity is O ( | A | + L ) , where | A | represents the size of the action space and L denotes the number of hierarchical levels. The per-episode complexity was O ( T ( | A | + L )) , where T is the episode length. The space complexity is O ( | S || A | L ) , which is primarily determined by the storage of Q-values across different levels. The algorithm achieves efficiency through three key mechanisms: state-space reduction via hierarchical decomposition, computation reuse through value propagation, and adaptive parameter adjustment based on uncertainty levels. 4.4. Fuzzy decision-making and resource allocation In this section, we propose a comprehensive fuzzy decision-making framework seamlessly integrated with our hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) agent. This framework introduces three key innovations: a multilevel fuzzy inference system (FIS) designed to process uncertain- ties across different time scales, an adaptive rule generation mechanism that synthesizes expert-defined rules with those learned from data, and a hierarchical integration scheme that effectively fuses fuzzy decisions with reinforcement learning policies. 4.4.1. Multilevel fuzzy inference system design The Fuzzy Inference System (FIS) [ 39 ] bridges the output of the HRL agent and concrete resource management actions. Our FIS is organized as a three-level hierarchical system, with each addressing decision at different time scales: (1) Strategic Level FIS: Handles long-term decisions such as capacity planning and workload distribution across data centers (operating on the order of hours). (2) Tactical Level FIS: Manages medium-term decisions including VM scaling and migration within each data center (operating on the order of minutes). Applied Soft Computing 186 (2026) 114157 8 L. Chen, C. Jiang, Y. Huang et al. (3) Operational Level FIS: Addresses short-term decisions such as task scheduling and immediate resource adjustments (operating on the order of seconds). Each level in the framework consists of four key components: (1) a Fuzzification Interface that converts crisp inputs into fuzzy sets using adaptive membership functions; (2) a Dynamic Rule Base that is respon- sible for maintaining and updating fuzzy IF-THEN rules by combining expert knowledge with online learning; (3) a Context-Aware Inference Engine that performs fuzzy reasoning by considering the current system state and uncertainty levels; and (4) a Precision-Guided Defuzzification module that transforms fuzzy outputs into precise resource management commands. sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: This section provides a comprehensive analysis of FA-HRL’s theoret- ical contributions, practical implications, experimental insights, limita- tions, and future research directions, positioning the framework within the broader landscape of cloud resource optimization. Applied Soft Computing 186 (2026) 114157 15 L. Chen, C. Jiang, Y. Huang et al. 6.1. Theoretical contributions FA-HRL’s primary theoretical contribution of FA-HRL lies in its novel integration of fuzzy logic and hierarchical RL, which addresses the lim- itations of the existing CRMP approaches. Unlike traditional methods, such as static provisioning [ 8 ] or threshold-based autoscaling [ 9 ], which assume deterministic workload patterns, FA-HRL employs fuzzy work- load clustering and prediction to model multigranularity uncertainties. This approach leverages triangular fuzzy numbers and possibility theory to represent imprecise demands, thereby providing a robust mathemat- ical foundation for decision-making under uncertainty. Compared to deep RL (DRL) methods [ 42 ], which struggle with high-dimensional state spaces due to crisp state representations, FA-HRL’s hierarchi- cal agent architecture of FA-HRL decomposes state-action spaces into meta-controller, resource manager, and task scheduler levels, thereby reducing the curse of dimensionality. The fuzzy adaptive reward mecha- nism further enhances adaptability by dynamically balancing objectives (e.g., resource utilization, energy efficiency, and QoS), outperforming static reward designs in multiagent RL (MARL) approaches [ 14 ]. From a theoretical perspective, FA-HRL advances this field by bridg- ing two established paradigms: fuzzy control theory and RL. Fuzzy logic, rooted in Zadeh’s seminal work [ 32 ], excels in handling imprecise data, but lacks scalable learning capabilities. Conversely, hierarchical RL, as developed by Mao et al. [ 6 ], optimizes long-term decisions but often overlooks uncertainty modeling. FA-HRL’s synergy of these paradigms enables a unified framework that not only models uncertainties, but also learns adaptive policies across multiple timescales. This is demonstrated by the fuzzy Q-learning algorithm ( Algorithm 1 ), which incorporates uncertainty-aware exploration and value propagation to ensure con- vergence under bounded uncertainty. Such theoretical advancements provide a blueprint for future research on uncertainty-aware decision- making systems beyond cloud computing, such as IoT scheduling [ 24 ] or renewable energy optimization [ 25 ]. 6.2. Practical implications The practical significance of FA-HRL lies in its ability to enhance resource efficiency and service quality in real-world cloud environ- ments, delivering tangible benefits to cloud service providers (CSPs) and end users. Experimental results on Google’s cluster traces ( Section 5 ) demonstrate that FA-HRL achieves approximately 13 % higher resource utilization, 10 % lower task completion time, and 30 % improved QoS metrics compared to state-of-the-art methods such as MARL and HRL ( Tables 5 and 6 ). These improvements translate into significant cost savings for CSPs, as higher utilization reduces the need for overpro- visioning, which can account for up to 25 % of the operational costs in volatile workloads [ 4 ]. For end-users, the reduced task completion time and lower SLA violation rate (4.9 % vs. 7.2 % for MARL) en- sure faster response times and higher reliability, which are critical for latency-sensitive applications, such as web services or streaming platforms. FA-HRL’s robustness of FA-HRL to workload fluctuations is particu- larly valuable in dynamic cloud settings, where peak-to-average demand ratios can exceed 10:1. The fuzzy prediction module of the framework enables proactive resource allocation, achieving a response time of 30 s to workload spikes compared to 55 s for MARL. sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This study introduces the Fuzzy-Adaptive Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (FA-HRL) framework, a novel approach for robust cloud resource management in the face of workload un- certainties and dynamic demands. By synergistically integrating fuzzy logic with hierarchical reinforcement learning, FA-HRL addresses three Applied Soft Computing 186 (2026) 114157 16 L. Chen, C. Jiang, Y. Huang et al. critical challenges: modeling multigranularity uncertainties; coordi- nating decisions across virtual machines, clusters, and data centers; and adapting dynamically to workload fluctuations. The framework’s innovative components—fuzzy workload clustering and prediction, context-aware fuzzy adaptive reward mechanism, and fuzzy rule-based policy generation system—enable precise resource allocation and enhanced service quality in realistic cloud environments. Our comprehensive evaluation of Google’s cluster traces demon- strated FA-HRL’s superiority of FA-HRL over state-of-the-art methods, achieving approximately 13 % higher resource utilization, 10 % lower task completion time, and 30 % improved QoS metrics. These results, coupled with the framework’s robustness to workload spikes and scal- ability across large-scale infrastructure, underscore its ability to handle heterogeneous resources and dynamic demands. FA-HRL represents a significant advancement in cloud resource management, offering a the- oretically grounded and practically viable solution that paves the way for more efficient and reliable cloud systems.
